While the motion of the barge was dramatically reduced from that of a buoy or ship due to its mooring system, multiple inertial motion units (IMU) were used to compensate barge data for those motions that existed. Key to the at-sea field components and central within the study area, the WFIP3 barge was moored in place, self-powered, and unattended, hosting sensors and instruments from WHOI, DOE-lab, and NOAA 13 partners as well as those from complementary projects funded by the DOE and the Bureau of Ocean and Energy Management (BOEM). The heavy mooring system specially designed for the WFIP3 barge spanned 1 NM2 in area, required dedicated winches and handling equipment on the barge, and multiple vessels to deploy, maintain, and recover. Anchor systems were pre-deployed from a separate crane barge beginning in early June, and all anchor components were removed by November. As designed, the mooring system was rated to hold the barge in place in significant wave heights up to 5 m (15'). The barge was mobilized in April and May of 2024, deployed in June, and recovered for the last time in late September. Weather-related recoveries accounted for 28 days of missed on-station time within the mobilization period. While on station, all deployed instruments or data systems were able to report data to the DOE Wind Data Hub in real time via satellite communications. Fig. 6. WFIP3 barge on deployment showing the mooring system and power components. The barge platform was deployed 25-NM south of Martha’s Vineyard during the summer of 2024. The purpose-built hybrid solar-battery-diesel power system was installed to power the 7-kW total sensor load continuously, without interruption, as a self-contained system for the entirety of the mobilization period. The power system utilized: 30 kW of solar panels (75 individual 400 W panels) mounted on raised supports above the barge deck (Fig. 6); an integrated 100 kWhr uninterruptible power supply and battery system composed of 5 separate 20 kW battery/inverters connected in parallel with a common controller; and two, linked, industrial 40 kW diesel generators for backup charging and emergency power. These components were integrated onto the barge by WHOI, who ran the barge deployment, power, and communications system for the deployment period. 14 Fig. 7. SHIP TRANSECTS AND SOUNDINGS Throughout the 18-month field deployment period, six intensive operating periods (IOPs) were organized around opportunistic vessel transects through the study area, project-specific offshore sampling via the barge, or a NOAA research vessel deployment to the same central site. Within each period (Table 4) radiosondes were launched from a land site in Woods Hole, MA as well as vessels offshore during three of the six periods. During the Spring and Fall 2024 periods, a ship transecting the study area from north to south (Fig. 1) launched atmospheric soundings at the same times as the land-based soundings as well as collected observations on the cloud and wind conditions via ceilometers and scanning and profiling Doppler lidars.
